components.note: 忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gàosu wǒ xiànzài de qíngkuàng.
example.english: Please tell me the current situation.
example.fact: 况 also stands on its own as a formal adverb meaning 'moreover, furthermore' (何况, 况且) — a reminder that a character's contribution inside a compound word doesn't always match what it means as an independent word.

components.note: 糸 (thread/silk) — 系 relates to connecting or tying things together, like threads linking into a system.

example.fact: 关系 covers far more ground than English 'relationship' — it's also the word behind "guānxi," the social capital and personal connections that grease business and favors in Chinese culture, so 有关系 can mean anything from 'related' to 'well-connected.'

components.note: 直 (straight, upright) — 真 relates to something level and true.
几 (a small table) — an object placed level and true on a table gave 真 its meaning 'real' or 'true.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.pinyin: Zhēnshi, nǐ yòu wàng dài yàoshi le.
example.english: Honestly, you forgot your keys again.
example.fact: On its own, 真是 can stand as a complete interjection of mild exasperation ("真是!"), much like English "Honestly!" — a shift from its literal sense 'truly, indeed' that shows up constantly in casual complaints.

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.

example.fact: 女士 is the neutral, marital-status-blind term for "Ms./madam" — unlike 小姐 (also in this batch), which traditionally named an unmarried young woman but has picked up a slang sense of "sex worker" in mainland China, making 女士 the safer default today.

components.note: 马 (simplified from 馬) depicts a horse in profile, with its mane, legs, and tail visible — later simplified into just a few strokes.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.fact: A popular, though linguistically disputed, folk etymology traces 马上 ('immediately') to imperial messengers who were already mounted and riding off — literally 'on the horse' (马 'horse' + 上 'on/above') — before finishing what they had to say.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.fact: 决定 works as a verb ('to decide') and a noun ('a decision', as in 做决定) without changing form at all — the same zero-derivation trick behind other common verb-noun pairs like 工作 ('to work' / 'a job').

components.note: 冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.fact: 到 acts here as a resultative complement meaning 'successfully arrived at' — 见到 specifically marks that the seeing actually happened, the same pattern behind 找到 ('to find,' lit. 'seek-arrive') and 听到 ('to hear,' lit. 'listen-arrive').

components.note: 木 (tree) — relates directly to 根's meaning 'root (of a plant or tree).'
艮 (gèn) gives a sound hint — 根 is pronounced gēn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
木 (tree) — provides the base image of a tree.
一 (a line) marks the base of the trunk, highlighting the roots — giving 本 its meaning 'root, origin, source.'

example.english: This isn't a problem at all.
example.fact: 根本 starts life as a noun for 'root, foundation,' but slotted before 不 in a negative sentence it turns into an intensifier meaning 'not... at all' (根本不是) — an adverbial use that often surprises learners who first meet the word as a noun.

example.hanzi: 这是一本关于历史的书。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì běn guānyú lìshǐ de shū.
example.english: This is a book about history.
example.fact: 关于 fronts the topic at the start of the phrase it introduces and can never be stranded at the end of a sentence the way English "about" can ("what's it about?") — the whole 关于-phrase has to come before what it describes.

components.note: 儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.fact: 那儿 is the Beijing-flavored, r-suffixed twin of the more neutral 那里 — the same colloquial-vs-standard split already seen in 这里/这儿 for "here" — a register choice rather than a difference in meaning.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the source of speech.
八 here suggests something small or simple leaving the mouth, giving 只 its meaning 'only, merely.'
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.pinyin: Zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.
example.english: As long as you work hard, you can succeed.
example.fact: 只要 almost never appears alone — it sets up a sufficient condition completed later in the sentence by 就 ("then"), forming the paired frame 只要...,就..., a structural cousin of 因为...所以... and 虽然...但是....

meanings: variant of 裡面|里面[li3 mian4]

components.note: 田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.
面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.fact: 里面 follows the noun it locates rather than preceding it ("箱子里面," literally "box inside") — like 上面 and 外面, it behaves more like a postposition than the preposition English "inside" is.

meanings: when all is said and done

components.note: 至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào
广 (a building/shelter) — 底 relates to the base or bottom, as of a structure
氐 (dǐ) gives the sound — 底 is also pronounced dǐ, an exact match

example.english: What exactly are you trying to say?
example.fact: 到底 shows up constantly in impatient or emphatic questions ("到底是谁?" "Who exactly is it?") — its literal image, "to the bottom," matches the English idiom "get to the bottom of it" almost exactly.

components.note: Depicts a child wrapped in swaddling, related to 子 (child); the picture-meaning has nothing to do with its modern grammatical role marking a completed action or change of state.
角 (horn) — 解 pictures removing a part of an animal.
牛 (ox) — together with a knife cutting between horn and ox, 解 pictures separating something into parts, giving its meaning 'to untie' or 'to explain.'

example.english: I want to understand you better.
example.fact: 了 is read liǎo here, not the far more common particle reading le — one of a handful of high-frequency characters (also 还 hái/huán, 觉 jué/jiào) whose pronunciation depends entirely on which word it is part of.

components.note: 日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.fact: 明 (built from 日 'sun' plus 月 'moon' — the two brightest things in the sky, together meaning 'bright') combines with 天 ('day') to give 明天 a still-visible logic: 'the bright/next day,' the same 明+[time word] pattern behind 明年 ('next year').

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 结 relates to tying or knotting threads together.
吉 (jí) gives a hint of the sound — 结 is pronounced jié, a connection that has shifted over time.
木 (wood) — 束 depicts a bundle of wood.
口 here depicts a rope or band wrapped around the wood, binding it together, giving 束 its meaning 'to bind, a bundle.'

example.fact: 结束 pairs two separate images of closure — 结 ('to knot,' from the thread radical 纟) and 束 (a bundle of wood bound with rope) — into a compound that reads almost literally as 'tied up and bundled,' i.e. wrapped up and finished.

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
司 depicts a person with a raised arm giving orders — an official directing others, giving rise to the meaning 'to manage' or 'to take charge of.'

example.hanzi: 我在一家外国公司工作。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài yì jiā wàiguó gōngsī gōngzuò.
example.english: I work at a foreign company.
example.fact: 公司 pairs 公 ('public, shared') with 司 ('to manage, to take charge of') — literally 'a publicly-run undertaking,' a fitting label for the modern idea of a jointly-owned commercial enterprise.

example.pinyin: Tā chéngwéi le yì míng yīshēng.
example.fact: 成为 is reserved for becoming a noun or role ('成为医生,' 'become a doctor') — for becoming an adjective or state, Chinese switches to 变得 ('变得更好,' 'become better'), a split English's single word 'become' doesn't make.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 远's meaning 'far, distant,' a long way to walk.
元 (yuán) gives a sound hint — 远 is pronounced yuǎn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.fact: 远 (built on the 'walking' radical 辶, evoking a long road) contributes 'far, distant' — paired with 永 ('perpetual'), 永远 projects that image of physical distance onto time, arriving at 'forever.'

components.note: 邦 (a nation/state) — a community bound together
巾 (a flag/cloth) — a banner people rally around to support one another
力 (strength) — 助 relates to helping, lending one's strength
且 (qiě) gives a loose sound connection to 助's reading zhù

example.fact: 帮助 doubles up two independently meaningful roots for 'help' — 帮 (from 邦 'a state, nation' plus 巾 'a banner,' picturing a flag people rally around) and 助 (力 'strength' lent to someone) — the same synonym-compounding strategy behind words like 喜欢 and 应该.

meanings: (after 对/就 + a noun or pronoun) as far as ... is concerned

components.note: Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.hanzi: 对我来说,这是一个很难的决定。
example.pinyin: Duì wǒ láishuō, zhè shì yí gè hěn nán de juédìng.
example.english: As far as I'm concerned, this is a difficult decision.
example.fact: 来说 never stands alone — it is the back half of the fixed frame 对/就 + [topic] + 来说 ("as far as X is concerned"), one of Mandarin's most common ways to frame a personal viewpoint before stating a claim, roughly matching English "-wise" or "in terms of."

components.note: 夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'
少 depicts a few small dots or grains, like scattered sand — a simple picture of a small quantity, giving the meaning 'few' or 'little.'

example.fact: 多少 and 几 both ask 'how many/how much,' but 几 expects a small, countable answer under about ten (几个人, 'a handful of people'), while 多少 carries no such ceiling — a scope distinction English's single question 'how many' doesn't mark.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē māo, tāmen dōu hěn kě'ài.
example.english: These cats — they're all very cute.
example.fact: Mandarin's third-person plural quietly splits by referent — 他们 for people or mixed groups, 她们 for all-female groups, 它们 for animals or things — even though all three are pronounced identically, tāmen; the distinction exists only in writing.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.
宀 (roof) — represents a home or fixed dwelling.
疋 (a foot/person) — a person settling down under a roof gave 定 its meaning 'to decide, to fix, to settle.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ quèdìng yào zǒu zhè tiáo lù ma?
example.english: Are you sure you want to take this road?
example.fact: 确定 slides between adjective ("certain, sure") and verb ("to confirm, to fix") depending on context — 你确定吗? asks "are you sure?," while 确定时间 means "to fix the time" — one word covering two different English parts of speech.

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.pinyin: Mén wài yǒurén zài děng nǐ.
example.english: There's someone waiting for you outside the door.
example.fact: 有人 doubles as the standard sign for an occupied public restroom, the mirror opposite of 没人 ("vacant, no one") — a practical, everyday use of the phrase well beyond its literal meaning "there is a person."

components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 清's meaning 'clear (water), pure.'
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 清 is also pronounced qīng, an exact match.

example.fact: 清楚 attaches after a verb as a resultative complement marking that the action was carried out to a clear, thorough degree — 说清楚 ('explain clearly'), 想清楚 ('think it through') — filling the same grammatical slot as 完 ('finish') or 好 ('well') after other verbs.

components.note: 日 (sun) — the sun is what disappears as evening falls
免 (to escape, avoid) — pictured as the sun slipping away, giving 晚 its sense of 'late, evening'
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.english: Let's have dinner together in the evening.
example.fact: 晚 is built from 日 ('sun') plus 免, traditionally read as the sun 'slipping away' — giving 晚 its sense of lateness, the same root behind 晚安 ('good night') and 晚点 ('running late').

components.note: 宀 (a roof, house) — 安 pictures shelter.
女 (woman) — a woman safely inside a house gave 安 its meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'
入 (enter, put away) — 全 pictures something being placed into safekeeping.
玉 (jade) — a valuable treasure kept whole and undamaged, giving 全 its meaning of 'complete' or 'entire.'

example.english: Pay attention to safety when driving.
example.fact: 安 (a woman 女 sheltered under a roof 宀, an image of domestic peace) contributes 'at ease, secure,' while 全 (a treasure 玉 kept whole and undamaged) contributes 'complete, intact' — together painting safety as being both protected and unharmed.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 怎's meaning 'how' relates to a mental inquiry, what's on one's mind.
乍 (zhà) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zěn.
木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.fact: 怎样 and its slightly longer cousin 怎么样 are near-interchangeable ways to ask "how/what's it like" — native speakers swap freely between them, though 怎么样 dominates casual speech while 怎样 reads a touch more formal or literary.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.
亻 (person) — 什 originally referred to a group of people.
十 (ten) — combined with 亻 (person), 什 originally described a group of ten; the character later came to be used for the common word 什么 (what).

example.fact: 没什么, taken apart, literally says "doesn't have what" (没 "not have" + 什么 "what") — from there it drifted into a fixed conversational reflex for waving off an apology or thanks, the same kind of semantic bleaching English's "it's nothing" has gone through.

components.note: 回 depicts a spiral or winding shape — something that turns back on itself, giving rise to the meaning 'to return.'
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.english: I go home at six every day.
example.fact: 回家 fuses the directional verb 回 ('to return') straight onto its destination 家 ('home') with no preposition in between — Chinese verb-object compounds like this routinely skip the 'to' that English inserts before a destination.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 愿 relates to a heartfelt wish or desire
原 (yuán) gives a loose sound connection to 愿's reading yuàn
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.

example.fact: 愿意 is built on the heart radical 心 in 愿, marking it as willingness that comes from one's own desire — distinct from 可以 ('is permitted to') or 能 ('is able to'), 愿意 is specifically about consent, not permission or capability.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 计 relates to counting or planning through words and numbers.
十 (shí) gives a hint of the sound — 计 is pronounced jì, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 我们的旅行计划改变了。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de lǚxíng jìhuà gǎibiàn le.
example.fact: 计 (built on the speech radical 讠 plus 十, since counting was once reckoned aloud) contributes 'to calculate, to reckon,' while 划 contributes 'to delineate, to map out' — together giving 计划 its literal sense of 'to reckon and lay out.'

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'

example.fact: Chinese runs three separate "can'ts" alongside its three "can's" — 可以 (permission), 会 (learned skill), 能 (ability/circumstance) — so 不可以 means "not allowed," 不会 means "don't know how," and 不能 means "not able to right now," each negating a different flavor of "can."

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 也 (also/additionally) — historically meant 'another person,' which developed into the third-person pronoun 'he/him.'
女 (woman) — 妈 refers to one's mother
马 (mǎ) gives a sound close to 妈's reading mā, differing only in tone

example.fact: 他妈的 is one of Mandarin's most common curse interjections, built literally from "his mother's" (他 "his" + 妈 "mother" + 的, the possessive particle) — an ellipsis of a much cruder insult about someone's mother, worn down by generations of casual use into a general-purpose expletive closer in force to English "damn it" than to its literal, far more offensive roots.

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.fact: 说话 is a verb-object compound that literally means 'to speak speech' — 话 already means 'words, speech' on its own, so the verb 说 ('to say') takes its own near-synonym as a built-in object, letting 说话 function as a self-contained verb for 'to talk.'

components.note: 女 (woman) — marks this pronoun as specifically feminine.
也 was already used as a gender-neutral third-person pronoun; adding 女 to it created a new character specifically for 'she.'
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.pinyin: Tāmen shì wǒ de hǎo péngyou.
example.fact: 她 didn't exist before the early 20th century — Chinese had no gendered third-person pronoun until 女 was added to the existing pronoun 也/他 to coin a dedicated character for "she," under pressure from translating Western literature; 她们 is simply the plural built on that comparatively young character.

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
二 (two) — 些 originally suggested a small plural amount, building on the idea of 'more than one.'
此 (cǐ) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches the modern reading xiē.

example.hanzi: 有些人不喜欢辣的食物。
example.pinyin: Yǒuxiē rén bù xǐhuan là de shíwù.
example.english: Some people don't like spicy food.
example.fact: 有些 can modify a noun ("有些人," "some people") or slide in front of an adjective to soften it into "somewhat, rather" ("有些累," "rather tired") — the same dual noun-quantifier/degree-adverb behavior shared by its near-synonym 一些.

components.note: 咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'
讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.

example.pinyin: Wǒ fēicháng gǎnxiè nǐ de bāngzhù.
example.english: I'm very grateful for your help.
example.fact: 感谢 sits a register above the everyday, reduplicated 谢谢 — reserved for more sincere or formal gratitude (speeches, thank-you letters, public acknowledgments), while 谢谢 handles the reflexive "thanks" of daily conversation.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谈 relates to talking, conversation
炎 (yán) gives a sound close to 谈's reading tán
讠 (speech) — 谈 relates to talking, conversation
炎 (yán) gives a sound close to 谈's reading tán

example.fact: 谈谈 reduplicates the verb 谈 ('to talk, converse') into a softer, more casual invitation — the same tone-softening reduplication behind 看看 ('take a look') and 谢谢 itself, where doubling a single-syllable verb makes the action feel brief and low-pressure.

example.english: Let's keep in touch more from now on.
example.fact: 以后 can attach after a time word or clause to mean "after X" (毕业以后, "after graduating"), or stand alone at the front of a sentence meaning simply "from now on" — two distinct grammatical slots for one word, told apart only by whether anything precedes it.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — relates to 照's meaning 'to shine, illuminate; photograph.'
昭 (zhāo) gives a sound hint — 照 is pronounced zhào, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
A pictograph of half of a split tree trunk, shown in cross-section (compare 爿, the other half) — the source of 片's meaning 'a thin slice, piece.'

example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒmen de jiéhūn zhàopiàn.
example.fact: 照 (built on the fire/light radical 灬, since photography is literally light striking a surface) contributes 'to shine, to capture light,' and 片 contributes 'a thin, flat piece' — together 照片 reads almost like 'a piece with light captured on it,' a fittingly literal description of what a photograph physically is.

components.note: 母 (mǔ, 'mother') serves as the phonetic base; the sound has since diverged from měi, so the connection is mostly historical today.
丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.hanzi: 每个人都有自己的想法。
example.pinyin: Měige rén dōu yǒu zìjǐ de xiǎngfǎ.
example.fact: 每 almost always needs a measure word directly after it before a noun — 每个人 ("every person"), 每天 ("every day," where 天 itself already functions as its own measure word) — a bare "每人" without a classifier sounds noticeably clipped next to English's classifier-free "every person."

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 迎 describes walking out to meet and welcome someone.
卬 (áng) gives a sound distantly related to yíng, having drifted apart over time.

example.fact: 迎 (built on the walking radical 辶, picturing someone walking out to receive a guest) contributes 'to go out and meet, to greet,' while 欢 simply contributes 'joyful' — together 欢迎 reads almost literally as 'to joyfully go out and meet [someone].'

meanings: I, me (humble term used by men in public speech)

components.note: 口 (mouth) pictures someone speaking.
儿 (person) below gives the shape of a person, together showing an elder brother speaking to his siblings.

example.fact: 兄弟 can narrow to mean specifically "younger brother," broaden to "brothers" in general, or — used self-referentially by men in informal speech — serve as a humble, matey stand-in for "I/me," a register-dependent range no single English gloss fully captures.

components.note: 人 (person), doubled — one person shown following another depicts the idea of accompanying or coming from somewhere.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.fact: 从来 almost always pairs with a negative (从来不, 从来没) to mean "never" — used without negation, it flips to the opposite meaning, "always, all along" (从来如此, "it's always been this way"), so the sentence's polarity completely changes the word's English translation.

components.note: 口 (mouths) — 总 pictures many voices.
心 (heart, mind) — many mouths brought together under one mind gave 总 its meaning 'overall' or 'to gather together.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.fact: 总是 marks a stable, repeated habit ('she's always busy') — for one unbroken, continuous state rather than a repeated pattern, Chinese instead reaches for 一直 ('continuously, all along'), a habitual-vs-continuous split that English 'always' flattens into one word.

meanings: to request sb to do sth

components.note: 手 (hand), shown twice, side by side — two hands pressed together in a gesture of respect, giving 拜 its meaning 'to bow, to pay respects.'
扌 (hand) — a hand held out, palm up
乇 — something resting on the upturned palm for support

example.pinyin: Bàituō, bāng wǒ yí gè máng!
example.fact: 拜托 literally combines 拜 ('to bow,' pictured as two hands pressed together in respect) with 托 ('to entrust,' held up on an open palm) — 'to bow and entrust a matter to someone' — and today also works as a stand-alone interjection of pleading, much like English 'please!' or 'come on!'

components.note: 女 depicts a kneeling figure with arms crossed, a traditional posture — a simple picture of a woman.
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.pinyin: Tāmen de nǚ'ér jīnnián wǔ suì.
example.english: Their daughter is five years old this year.
example.fact: 女儿 is built as 女 ('female') plus 儿, the very same suffix that independently means 'child, son' in 儿子 ('son') — making 女儿 transparently 'female child,' a mirror image of how 儿子 uses that same 儿.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
女 (woman) — 姐 names a female relative, an older sister.
且 (qiě) gives the rhyme, close to jiě though the tone differs.

example.fact: 小姐 traditionally addressed any young, usually unmarried woman and still works as the standard polite way to address a waitress or shop assistant in Taiwan and Hong Kong — but in mainland China it has also picked up a slang sense of "sex worker," which is why many mainland speakers now prefer the safer 女士 (also in this batch) instead.
